sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Chest x-ray in a young man following a motor vehicle crash (MVC) shows a pneumothorax, chest tube, and nasogastric (NG) tube that is curved up toward the chest.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-01

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CT in the same patient shows the typical signs of diaphragmatic injury, including the fallen viscus sign. The stomach lies in the chest. Note that it has "fallen" medially and posteriorly to lie against the posteromedial chest wall. The stomach appears pinched as it traverses the defect in the diaphragm (collar sign).
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-02

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CECT shows the stomach in the thorax; it has "fallen" through the diaphragmatic defect to lie against the posteromedial chest wall. The anterior wall of the stomach directly abuts the lung and is not confined by the diaphragm.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-03

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Coronal CECT in the same patient demonstrates the stomach extending upward through a diaphragmatic defect.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-04

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CECT in a patient following a MVC shows the stomach lying too far medial, posterior, and superior, indicating herniation through the diaphragm. This is the fallen viscus sign.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-05

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CECT in a patient after a stab wound demonstrates a splenic laceration with hematoma, left hemothorax , and subcutaneous emphysema . The presence of hematoma above and below the left diaphragm was concerning for diaphragmatic injury, subsequently confirmed at surgery.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-06

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Coronal CECT in a trauma patient demonstrates a gap in the left hemidiaphragm with the colon protruding into the thorax. Note the extensive enteric contrast material throughout the left thorax due to colonic perforation.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-07

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Sagittal T2 MR demonstrates diaphragmatic injury due to surgical error. A tear is seen in the left hemidiaphragm with the stomach herniating into the chest. The diaphragm is identified as a low-signal curvilinear structure with a central gap.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-08

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CECT in a trauma patient demonstrates that the stomach is "pinched" as it traverses a defect in the left diaphragm. Another sign of diaphragmatic rupture is abdominal fat outside the confines of the diaphragm (in the thorax).
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-09

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Coronal CECT after trauma demonstrates splenic injury with active extravasation , left-sided hemothorax , and lung contusion . Injuries above and below the diaphragm raise concern for diaphragmatic injury, as evidenced by a small defect in the left diaphragm .
sourceQualifiedImages.label: RP-10

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CECT shows the stomach in the thorax, which has "fallen" through the diaphragmatic defect to lie against the posteromedial chest wall . The anterior wall of the stomach directly abuts the lung and is not confined by the diaphragm.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: SDX-03

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Sagittal CECT in the same patient demonstrates the stomach extending upward through a diaphragmatic defect. The anterior wall of the stomach directly contacts the lung, confirming the presence of a traumatic diaphragmatic hernia.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: SDX-04

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CECT in a trauma patient demonstrates a loop of bowel extending upward and directly contacting the heart.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: SDX-05

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Coronal CECT in the same patient demonstrates the intact left hemidiaphragm , while the right diaphragm is disrupted with omental fat and bowel extending upward adjacent to the heart. At surgery, the duodenum and omental fat were found within the pericardial sac, herniating through a defect in the diaphragm and pericardium.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: SDX-06

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Coronal T2 MR demonstrates diaphragmatic injury due to surgical error. A tear is seen in the left hemidiaphragm with the stomach herniating into the chest. The diaphragm is identified as a low-signal curvilinear structure with a central gap.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: SDX-10

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CECT at lung windows shows splenic flexure of the colon abutting the lung and pneumothorax.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: SDX-11

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CECT shows the spleen in a dependent position and abdominal fat lateral to the diaphragm .
sourceQualifiedImages.label: SDX-12

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CECT shows the dependent viscus with the colon and abdominal fat lying lateral to the diaphragm , indicating the thoracic position.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: SDX-13

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Chest radiograph shows an "elevated," distorted diaphragm and the high position of the NG tube .
sourceQualifiedImages.label: SDX-14

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CECT shows the "dependent" viscus sign with the spleen and bowel abutting the posterior ribs.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: SDX-17

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Chest radiograph shows an "elevated" and indistinct left hemidiaphragm. The tip of the NG tube is pointed up.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: SDX-18

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Chest radiograph in a 66-year-old man following an MVC shows a high and distorted left hemidiaphragm, or abnormal intrathoracic contents, with the NG tube curled back up, indicating a high position of the stomach.
sourceQualifiedImages.label: SDX-19

sourceQualifiedImages.caption: Axial CT in the same patient shows the fallen viscus sign with the stomach lying adjacent to the spine and posterior chest wall, instead of being suspended by the left hemidiaphragm. Note the NG tube .
sourceQualifiedImages.label: SDX-20
